lessons.title: The OSI Model: Seven Layers of Networking
lessons.chapterTitle: Networking Fundamentals I: The OSI & TCP/IP Models

slots.practicalActivity: On your own computer, run ipconfig /all (Windows) or ip addr (Linux/Mac) to see your real MAC address and IP address, then run tracert (or traceroute) to a real site like google.com. For each of the first 3 hops, label whether you're looking at Layer 1 (link up/down), Layer 2 (MAC-based forwarding before your gateway), or Layer 3 (IP-based routing after your gateway) information, then write 2-3 sentences reproducing the mnemonic (Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away) from memory, bottom to top.
slots.deliverable: Real ipconfig/ip addr and tracert/traceroute output from your own machine, each hop labeled with the OSI layer it corresponds to, plus the full 7-layer mnemonic reproduced correctly from memory.

lessons.title: The TCP/IP Model and How It Maps to OSI
lessons.chapterTitle: Networking Fundamentals I: The OSI & TCP/IP Models

slots.practicalActivity: Capture a single real HTTP or HTTPS request leaving your own machine (Wireshark, or your browser's dev-tools Network tab for the application layer) and identify the four TCP/IP layers in order: the Ethernet frame (Network Access), the IP packet (Internet), the TCP segment (Transport), and the HTTP/HTTPS payload (Application). Then write a translation exercise: rewrite 'this firewall rule operates at Layer 4' in TCP/IP vocabulary, and rewrite 'the Internet layer handles this' in OSI vocabulary.
slots.deliverable: A short written breakdown identifying all 4 TCP/IP layers in one real captured request, plus both direction translations between OSI and TCP/IP vocabulary for the Layer 4 / Internet layer example.

lessons.title: Network Topologies and Physical Media
lessons.chapterTitle: Networking Fundamentals I: The OSI & TCP/IP Models

slots.practicalActivity: Sketch your own home or workplace network's real topology (almost certainly a star, with your router/switch at the center), noting how many devices connect to it. Inspect the printed label on a real cable running to your own desktop and identify whether it's Cat5e, Cat6, or Cat6a. Then calculate a full-mesh connection count for your own real device count using n(n-1)/2 to see how fast that would get unreasonable.
slots.deliverable: A written sketch/description of your own real network's star topology, the real cable category found on an inspected cable, and the full-mesh connection-count calculation for your actual device count.

lessons.title: Ethernet, MAC Addresses, and Switching Basics
lessons.chapterTitle: Networking Fundamentals I: The OSI & TCP/IP Models

slots.practicalActivity: Run ipconfig /all (Windows) or ip link (Linux) to find your own machine's real MAC address, split it into its 6 hex pairs, and identify the first 3 bytes (the OUI) — then look up that OUI prefix online to identify the manufacturer. Write out, step by step, the learn-then-forward process a switch uses the first time two of your real devices (e.g. laptop and phone) talk to each other on your home network.
slots.deliverable: Your own real MAC address with the OUI identified to a manufacturer, plus a written step-by-step walkthrough of switch learning/flooding/forwarding applied to two of your own real devices.

lessons.title: IPv4 Addressing and Subnetting
lessons.chapterTitle: Networking Fundamentals II: IP Addressing & Routing

slots.practicalActivity: By hand, with no subnet calculator, work out the network address, broadcast address, and usable host range for 10.0.5.0/28 exactly as the lesson's check-yourself question asks, showing your work: host bits, total addresses, and block size. Then find your own home network's real subnet mask (check your router's settings or ipconfig/ip addr) and calculate how many usable hosts it supports.
slots.deliverable: A fully worked-by-hand subnet calculation for 10.0.5.0/28 (network, broadcast, usable range) plus the same calculation applied to your own real home network's subnet mask.

lessons.title: IPv6 Addressing Fundamentals
lessons.chapterTitle: Networking Fundamentals II: IP Addressing & Routing

slots.practicalActivity: Run ipconfig /all (Windows) or ip addr (Linux/Mac) and find your own machine's real IPv6 link-local address (starts with fe80::). Write it out in both full form and shortened form. Then take the lesson's example address 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:ff00:0042:8329 and shorten it yourself by hand, applying both the leading-zero and :: rules, and check your answer against 2001:db8::ff00:42:8329.
slots.deliverable: Your own real fe80:: link-local IPv6 address shown in both full and shortened form, plus your own hand-worked shortening of the lesson's example address matching 2001:db8::ff00:42:8329.

lessons.title: Routing Basics: How Packets Find Their Way
lessons.chapterTitle: Networking Fundamentals II: IP Addressing & Routing

slots.practicalActivity: Find your own device's real default gateway (ipconfig or ip route) and ping it to confirm it responds. Run tracert/traceroute to a real external site, count the hops, and write one sentence for each of the first 3 hops about what network it's probably crossing. Then write a short paragraph explaining, using the lesson's /32 vs /24 vs /0 example, why a router always picks the most specific matching route.
slots.deliverable: A successful ping to your own real default gateway, a tracert/traceroute to an external site with each early hop annotated, and a written explanation of most-specific-route-wins using the /32 vs /24 vs /0 example.

lessons.title: NAT, DHCP, and DNS in Practice
lessons.chapterTitle: Networking Fundamentals II: IP Addressing & Routing

slots.practicalActivity: Run ipconfig /release then ipconfig /renew (Windows) or sudo dhclient -r && sudo dhclient (Linux) on a device you control to force a real DORA exchange, then check ipconfig /all or ip addr afterward to confirm the lease. Run nslookup or dig against a real domain to watch DNS resolution happen. Then compare your device's private IP against your router's public WAN IP to see NAT in action.
slots.deliverable: Proof of a real DHCP release/renew cycle (DORA) on your own device, an nslookup/dig DNS resolution of a real domain, and a side-by-side comparison of your device's private IP vs. your router's public WAN IP demonstrating NAT.

lessons.title: TCP vs. UDP and the Three-Way Handshake

slots.practicalActivity: Open Wireshark (or tcpdump) and capture traffic while loading a single website in a browser. Find the 3 packets that make up the handshake and label them SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK with their sequence/ack numbers, matching the lesson's diagram. Then explain, referencing the lesson's VoIP example, why a real video call you've personally used (Zoom, FaceTime, etc.) tolerates a dropped packet without it looking like an error.
slots.deliverable: A real Wireshark/tcpdump capture with the SYN, SYN-ACK, and ACK packets of one TCP handshake identified and their sequence/ack numbers labeled, plus a written explanation of why UDP suits a real video call you've used.

lessons.title: Common Ports and Protocols Every Analyst Must Know

slots.practicalActivity: From memory, with no lookup, write out all 12 ports from the lesson's table with their protocol and purpose, then self-check against the lesson. Then run netstat -an (Windows) or ss -tulpn (Linux) on your own machine and find at least 3 real listening or established connections, identifying the port and matching protocol for each from memory.
slots.deliverable: The full 12-port table reproduced from memory and self-checked, plus real netstat/ss output from your own machine with at least 3 connections' ports correctly identified by protocol.

lessons.title: Network Services: Web, Email, File Transfer

slots.practicalActivity: Using a browser's developer tools (Network tab), load a real webpage and find the actual request method, status code, and headers for one HTTP request. Check your own email client's account settings to find which protocol it uses to retrieve mail (POP3 or IMAP) and which port, noting whether that matches synced-across-devices behavior you've observed. Then check whether your home router or NAS exposes an SMB share and note the path, or explain in one sentence why a work network drive uses SMB under the hood.
slots.deliverable: A real captured HTTP request/response (method, status code, headers) from your browser's dev tools, your own email client's actual retrieval protocol and port identified, and a written note on SMB file-sharing applied to a real or hypothetical network drive.

lessons.title: Wireless Networking and Wi-Fi Security Basics

slots.practicalActivity: On your own phone or laptop, check your home Wi-Fi's actual security setting (in the Wi-Fi connection details) and identify whether it's WPA2 or WPA3. If it's WPA2, write one sentence on what upgrading to WPA3 would specifically fix. Then use your phone's Wi-Fi scanner to list 3 real nearby SSIDs you can see and write one sentence on how you'd distinguish a legitimate network from an evil-twin impersonating one of them with an identical name.
slots.deliverable: Your own home Wi-Fi's actual security standard (WPA2/WPA3) identified from the device settings, a list of 3 real nearby SSIDs your device can see, and a written explanation of how to spot an evil-twin impersonating one of them.

lessons.title: The CIA Triad: Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability

slots.practicalActivity: Pick 3 real pieces of data from your own digital life (e.g. your bank balance, a personal photo, your email access) and for each one, write one sentence identifying which leg of the CIA triad matters most for it and why. Then write a full answer to the lesson's check-yourself scenario (a website stays online, no data stolen, but prices get silently changed) explaining why that's an integrity violation specifically, not confidentiality or availability.
slots.deliverable: 3 real personal data examples each mapped to a CIA triad leg with a justification, plus a full written answer to the silently-changed-prices scenario explaining why it is an integrity violation.

lessons.title: Threat Actors, Motivations, and Attack Surfaces

slots.practicalActivity: List your own personal attack surface as if you were the target: every internet-connected device you own, every account with a password, every app with access to your data, and any smart-home/IoT device. For 3 items, name one concrete action that would shrink the attack surface (disabling an unused service, deleting an old account, patching a device). Then classify, in one sentence each, which of the 5 threat-actor categories would most plausibly target you personally vs. a large bank.
slots.deliverable: Your own real personal attack-surface inventory with at least 3 concrete reduction actions identified, plus a written comparison of which threat-actor category would realistically target you versus a large bank.

lessons.title: Vulnerabilities, Threats, and Risk: How They Relate

slots.practicalActivity: Pick a real piece of software you personally use that you know is out of date (check Settings > About or an update checker). Write a mini risk assessment following Risk = Likelihood x Impact: name the vulnerability (the specific outdated version), the threat (who would realistically target it), and your own likelihood/impact rating with reasoning, concluding whether you should patch it today or it can wait.
slots.deliverable: A written risk assessment of one real outdated piece of software you personally use, naming the specific vulnerability, a plausible threat, and a reasoned Likelihood x Impact risk rating with a patch-now-or-later conclusion.

lessons.title: The Cybersecurity Kill Chain and the MITRE ATT&CK Framework

slots.practicalActivity: Write out all 7 stages of the Cyber Kill Chain from memory, in order, then self-check against the lesson. Then look up the real MITRE ATT&CK technique T1059 (Command and Scripting Interpreter) referenced in the lesson at attack.mitre.org, and write 2-3 sentences in your own words describing what it actually is and which kill-chain stage it would most likely appear at.
slots.deliverable: The 7 Cyber Kill Chain stages reproduced correctly from memory, plus a real MITRE ATT&CK technique lookup (T1059) with a written summary and the kill-chain stage you'd place it at.

lessons.title: Authentication Factors and Multi-Factor Authentication

slots.practicalActivity: Confirm real MFA is turned on using a TOTP authenticator app on one of your own actual accounts that supports it (email, bank, etc.) — open the app and watch a real 30-second code actually rotate. Then audit 3 of your own accounts and write down, for each, which factor or combination currently protects it, and whether any of them are still 'something you know' alone.
slots.deliverable: Confirmation of a real TOTP authenticator app in use on one of your own accounts with a code observed rotating, plus a written factor audit of 3 of your own real accounts identifying which are still single-factor.

lessons.title: Authorization Models: RBAC, DAC, MAC

slots.practicalActivity: Check the real sharing settings on one of your own files in Google Drive, OneDrive, or Dropbox and write down exactly who has access and at what level — that's DAC in action, under your own discretion as owner. If you have access to any system with role-based permissions (an LMS, a shared drive with security groups, a SaaS admin console), identify one real role and list 2 permissions it grants that a different role doesn't.
slots.deliverable: The real current sharing settings of one of your own cloud-storage files documented as a DAC example, plus one real role-based permission example from a system you have access to, naming 2 permissions tied to that role.

lessons.title: Symmetric vs. Asymmetric Encryption

slots.practicalActivity: Visit any HTTPS site and click the padlock icon in your browser's address bar to view the real certificate — note the issuing CA and the cipher suite listed under 'Connection is secure' > certificate details. Then write a short explanation, using the padlock analogy from the lesson, of what happened in the handshake before your browser switched to fast symmetric encryption for the rest of the page load.
slots.deliverable: A real HTTPS certificate's issuing CA and cipher suite inspected from your own browser on a real site, plus a written explanation of the asymmetric-then-symmetric handshake sequence using the padlock analogy.

lessons.title: Hashing, Digital Signatures, and PKI Basics

slots.practicalActivity: Using an online SHA-256 tool or your OS's built-in command (certutil -hashfile on Windows, shasum -a 256 on Mac/Linux), hash a real short text file twice to confirm you get the identical hash both times, then change one character and hash it again to see the output change completely. Then revisit the same HTTPS certificate from last session and trace its chain of trust up to the root CA shown in your browser's certificate viewer, writing down each certificate in the chain.
slots.deliverable: Real SHA-256 output showing an identical hash on two runs of the same file and a completely different hash after a 1-character change, plus a documented certificate chain of trust (leaf to root) from a real HTTPS site.

lessons.title: Malware Types: Viruses, Worms, Trojans, Ransomware

slots.practicalActivity: Using the lesson's 'telling them apart fast' table, write your own one-sentence classification test for each of the 4 categories (virus, worm, trojan, ransomware) applied to a hypothetical sample you make up. Then research one real, named malware incident from the last 5 years (not WannaCry or Melissa, already covered) and classify which category it belongs to based on its actual spreading behavior, citing your source.
slots.deliverable: Your own 4 classification test sentences (virus/worm/trojan/ransomware) applied to a hypothetical example, plus one real, cited malware incident from the last 5 years correctly classified by its actual spreading behavior.

lessons.title: Social Engineering: Phishing, Pretexting, and Baiting

slots.practicalActivity: Check your own email spam/junk folder for a real phishing or spear-phishing attempt you've received, and annotate it: what trusted sender is it impersonating, what action does it want you to take, and what specific detail gives it away. If you don't have one, find a real documented phishing example and annotate that instead. Then write your own 2-sentence pretexting scenario modeled on the lesson's 'traveling executive' example, set at a company or organization you're familiar with.
slots.deliverable: A real (or real-example) phishing email annotated with the impersonated sender, the requested action, and the giveaway details, plus an original 2-sentence pretexting scenario modeled on the lesson's example.

lessons.title: Network Attacks: MITM, DoS/DDoS, and Spoofing

slots.practicalActivity: Write out the specific indicator from the lesson's 'watching for the signs' section that distinguishes a DoS flood from a DDoS flood, and apply it to the lesson's own check-yourself scenario (all packets from one source IP). Then run arp -a (Windows) or ip neigh (Linux) on your own machine to see your real current ARP table, and write one sentence on what a sudden duplicate IP-to-MAC mapping in that table would indicate.
slots.deliverable: A written answer to the DoS-vs-DDoS check-yourself scenario citing the specific distinguishing indicator, plus your own real ARP table output with a written explanation of what a duplicate mapping would mean.

lessons.title: Web Application Attacks: Injection and XSS Basics

slots.practicalActivity: Find a real login or search/comment form you use regularly and, without submitting anything malicious, write where user input flows into it and what the application likely does with it on the backend (a database query for a login, a rendered display for a search/comment). Then explain how the single defensive principle — never trust user input — would need to apply specifically to that field, as either a parameterized query (SQLi) or output encoding (XSS).
slots.deliverable: A written analysis of a real form's input-handling path mapped to either a potential SQLi or XSS risk, plus a specific explanation of how parameterized queries or output encoding would need to apply to that exact field.

lessons.title: Defense in Depth and the Security Layered Model
lessons.chapterTitle: Security Policy, Governance & Defense in Depth

slots.practicalActivity: Pick a real account or device of your own (home Wi-Fi + router, or a work laptop) and list every actual security layer currently protecting it, mapped to the lesson's 5 layers (perimeter, network, endpoint, access control, monitoring). For any layer that's completely missing, write one sentence on what a minimal real-world version of it would look like for that exact device. Then answer the lesson's check-yourself question in writing: is one contractor managing every layer with identical default settings real defense in depth?
slots.deliverable: Your own real device or account mapped against all 5 defense-in-depth layers with gaps identified, plus a written answer to the single-contractor/default-settings check-yourself question.

lessons.title: Security Policies, Standards, and Acceptable Use
lessons.chapterTitle: Security Policy, Governance & Defense in Depth

slots.practicalActivity: If you have access to a real organization's actual Acceptable Use Policy or password policy (current or past employer, school), read it and pull out 3 real specific rules it states. If you don't have access to one, draft your own 4-sentence Acceptable Use Policy for a fictional 10-person company, matching the lesson's examples (unauthorized software, personal use of company email, USB devices). Then write the lesson's exact password-policy sentence and describe the specific technical settings an IT admin would configure to enforce it.
slots.deliverable: 3 real policy rules pulled from an actual organization's AUP/password policy (or an original 4-sentence AUP draft if none is accessible), plus a written mapping from the lesson's password-policy sentence to the specific technical settings that enforce it.

lessons.title: Compliance Frameworks: NIST, ISO 27001, and Why They Matter
lessons.chapterTitle: Security Policy, Governance & Defense in Depth

slots.practicalActivity: Write out the NIST Cybersecurity Framework's 5 functions from memory (Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover), then map 3 specific things you've already done in this course (building toward a home lab, learning encryption, learning incident-response policy) to the correct function. Then find one real company's published ISO 27001 certification announcement or compliance page and write 2 sentences on why that company likely pursued it, citing which of the lesson's 3 reasons (legal, customer trust, contractual) applies.
slots.deliverable: The NIST Framework's 5 functions reproduced from memory with 3 of your own course activities correctly mapped to them, plus a real company's ISO 27001 certification example with a written reason for pursuing it.

lessons.title: Physical Security and Environmental Controls
lessons.chapterTitle: Security Policy, Governance & Defense in Depth

slots.practicalActivity: Walk through your own home or workplace and identify 3 real physical security measures actually in place (a locked door, a camera, a visitor sign-in sheet, anything) and 1 real gap you notice. For the gap, write one sentence on which leg of the CIA triad it threatens and why. Then find which cloud provider (AWS, Azure, or GCP) publishes details about their data centers' physical security and summarize one real control they describe (badge access, mantraps, or environmental controls) in 2 sentences.
slots.deliverable: 3 real physical security measures and 1 real gap identified at your own home or workplace with the gap mapped to a CIA triad leg, plus a real cloud provider's published physical-security control summarized in your own words.

lessons.title: Building a Home Lab for Security Practice

slots.practicalActivity: Install VirtualBox (free) on your own computer, download and import a real Kali Linux VM image, and boot it — confirm you can log in and run uname -a inside it. Download and import Metasploitable2 as a second VM, and before powering it on, set both VMs' network adapters to Host-Only (or Internal Network in VMware), confirming neither is set to Bridged.
slots.deliverable: A real, booted Kali Linux VM with uname -a output proving it's running, a second Metasploitable2 VM imported alongside it, and both VMs' network adapter settings confirmed as Host-Only/Internal (never Bridged) before either is powered on together.

lessons.title: Packet Capture Basics: Reading Traffic with Wireshark

slots.practicalActivity: On your Kali VM from last session, open Wireshark, select the lab's network interface, and start a capture. Browse to Metasploitable2's web page (or ping it) to generate real traffic, then stop the capture, find one real TCP handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK), and label each packet's flags in the packet list. Apply the display filter tcp.port == 80 and confirm the view narrows to HTTP traffic only. Then run a quick Nmap scan from Kali against Metasploitable2 while still capturing, and find the SYN-with-no-reply pattern the lesson described as a port scan.
slots.deliverable: A real Wireshark capture showing a labeled 3-packet TCP handshake, the view successfully narrowed with a tcp.port == 80 display filter, and the SYN-flood/port-scan pattern from a real Nmap scan visible and identified in the same capture.

lessons.title: Case Study: Tracing an Attack Through the Kill Chain

slots.practicalActivity: Using the Fairmont Logistics case study's 6 stages as your template, invent your own realistic attack scenario against a fictional small business of your choosing (name it, give it an industry), and write one sentence per stage (Reconnaissance through Actions on Objectives) describing what the attacker does, plus one specific defense from this course — naming the actual lesson or control — that could have stopped that exact stage.
slots.deliverable: An original 6-stage kill-chain case study for your own fictional company, with one real attack action and one specific named defense (tied to an actual lesson/control from this course) written for every stage.

lessons.title: Chapter Capstone: Networking & Security Fundamentals Review

slots.practicalActivity: Using the lesson's 7:42 AM SIEM alert scenario as the model, write your own full incident-response narrative for a different, invented alert of your choice, walking it through all 4 phases: networking fundamentals (what you check first), core security concepts (CIA triad and risk framing), attack recognition (which Chapter 6 category it matches), and policy/defense (what your incident-response policy requires next). Then write a 1-paragraph self-assessment naming the chapter you feel least confident in and your specific plan (which lesson to re-watch, which lab to redo) to shore it up before the next course.
slots.deliverable: An original full incident narrative for an invented alert walked through all 4 phases (networking, core concepts, attack recognition, policy/defense) in the same structure as the lesson's example, plus a written self-assessment naming your weakest chapter and a specific concrete plan to address it.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: A student finishing this course can read and troubleshoot a network using the OSI/TCP-IP models, calculate IPv4 subnets by hand, recognize IPv6 addresses on sight, explain how DHCP, DNS, and NAT work together on any network they join, and recite the common ports and protocols a SOC shift requires memorized cold. They can reason precisely about the CIA triad, the difference between a vulnerability, a threat, and risk, and where a real incident sits on both the Cyber Kill Chain and in the MITRE ATT&CK catalog; distinguish authentication factors from authorization models (RBAC, DAC, MAC); and explain symmetric vs. asymmetric encryption, hashing, and the PKI chain of trust behind HTTPS. They can correctly classify malware (virus, worm, trojan, ransomware), social-engineering techniques, network attacks (MITM, DoS/DDoS, spoofing), and web attacks (SQL injection, XSS) from real-world indicators, and connect each one to the defense-in-depth layer, written policy, or compliance framework (NIST, ISO 27001) that should have stopped it. Most importantly, they've built and used a real isolated home lab — Kali Linux and Metasploitable2 in VirtualBox or VMware with host-only networking — captured and read live traffic in Wireshark including a real TCP handshake and a real Nmap port scan, and walked a full realistic attack through every kill-chain stage end to end, which is the exact hands-on foundation a SOC analyst role expects on day one.
